title: Killing the first variables of a power series ring
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative ring, $d\ge0$, $0\le i\le d$, and let $R=A[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]]$ and $R_i=A[[X_{i+1},\ldots,X_d]]$ be formal power series rings [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series], $R_i\subseteq R$ as the series involving only $X_{i+1},\ldots,X_d$ ($R_d=A$). Define $\pi_i:R\to R_i$ by $\pi_i\bigl(\sum_Ea_EX^E\bigr)=\sum_{E:\,e_1=\cdots=e_i=0}a_EX^E$. Then $\pi_i$ is a surjective homomorphism of $A$-algebras which is the identity on $R_i$, and its kernel is the ideal $(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$ of $R$. In particular ($i=d$) the constant coefficient map $F\mapsto F(0)$, $R\to A$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$, and $R/(X_1,\ldots,X_i)\cong A[[X_{i+1},\ldots,X_d]]$.

source.place: used without statement in Remark Tag 032C (remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, line 45023) for the dimension and the maximal ideal; agent-formulated

proof.text:
*Notation; $R_i$ is a subring.* By [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series] an element of $R$ is a family $F=(a_E)_{E\in\mathbf N^d}$ of elements of $A$, written $\sum_Ea_EX^E$, with coefficientwise sum and product $(FG)_H=\sum_{E+E'=H}a_Eb_{E'}$ for $G=(b_{E'})$; the unit is $X^0$ and $A	o R$ is $r\mapsto rX^0$. Let $S=\{E\in\mathbf N^d:e_1=\cdots=e_i=0\}$. The map $\mathbf N^{d-i}	o S$, $(e_{i+1},\ldots,e_d)\mapsto(0,\ldots,0,e_{i+1},\ldots,e_d)$, is a bijection compatible with addition, and $R_i\subseteq R$ is the set of families vanishing outside $S$ (via this bijection). Since exponents are $\ge0$, for $E,E'\in\mathbf N^d$ one has $E+E'\in S$ if and only if $E\in S$ and $E'\in S$. Hence if $F,G$ vanish outside $S$, then $(FG)_H=0$ for $H
otin S$ (every pair with $E+E'=H$ has $E
otin S$ or $E'
otin S$), and for $H\in S$ the sum $(FG)_H$ runs over pairs in $S	imes S$, which is the product of $A[[X_{i+1},\ldots,X_d]]$ transported by the bijection. So $R_i$ is a subring of $R$ containing $A$ ($rX^0$, $0\in S$), and the inclusion $R_i\subseteq R$ is a homomorphism of $A$-algebras; for $i=d$, $S=\{0\}$ and $R_d=A$.

source.place: Remark Tag 032C (remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, line 45023), where the fact is used without statement; the argument is written by an agent from the definition of the power series ring

proof.text: *$\pi_i$ is a homomorphism of $A$-algebras.* By definition $\pi_i(F)_E=a_E$ for $E\in S$ and $\pi_i(F)_E=0$ for $E\notin S$; its value vanishes outside $S$, so lies in $R_i$ (step 1). It is additive (sums are coefficientwise), and $\pi_i(X^0)=X^0$ since $0\in S$. For $r\in A$, $(rX^0\cdot F)_E=ra_E$ by the product formula, so $\pi_i(rF)=r\pi_i(F)$. Multiplicativity: let $F=(a_E)$, $G=(b_{E'})$ and $H\in\mathbf N^d$. If $H\notin S$, both $\pi_i(FG)_H$ and $(\pi_i(F)\pi_i(G))_H$ are $0$, the second by step 1 because $\pi_i(F),\pi_i(G)$ vanish outside $S$. If $H\in S$, every pair with $E+E'=H$ has $E,E'\in S$ (step 1), so $\pi_i(FG)_H=(FG)_H=\sum_{E+E'=H}a_Eb_{E'}=\sum_{E+E'=H}\pi_i(F)_E\pi_i(G)_{E'}=(\pi_i(F)\pi_i(G))_H$. Hence $\pi_i(FG)=\pi_i(F)\pi_i(G)$, and $\pi_i$ is an $A$-algebra homomorphism $R\to R_i$.

source.place: Remark Tag 032C (remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, line 45023), where the fact is used without statement; the argument is written by an agent from the definition of the power series ring

proof.text: *$\pi_i$ is the identity on $R_i$ and surjective.* If $F\in R_i$, i.e. $a_E=0$ for $E\notin S$, then $\pi_i(F)_E=a_E$ for every $E$, so $\pi_i(F)=F$. Hence every element of $R_i$ is its own image, and $\pi_i:R\to R_i$ is surjective.

source.place: Remark Tag 032C (remark-Noetherian-complete-local-ring-universally-catenary, line 45023), where the fact is used without statement; the argument is written by an agent from the definition of the power series ring

proof.text: *$(X_1,\ldots,X_i)\subseteq\ker\pi_i$.* For $j\le i$ the series $X_j$ is the family with coefficient $1$ at the unit vector $\varepsilon_j$ (whose $j$-th entry is $1$) and $0$ elsewhere; $\varepsilon_j\notin S$, so $\pi_i(X_j)=0$. Since $\pi_i$ is a ring homomorphism (step 2), $\pi_i(\sum_{j\le i}X_jG_j)=\sum_j\pi_i(X_j)\pi_i(G_j)=0$ for all $G_j\in R$, i.e. the ideal $(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$ lies in $\ker\pi_i$.

proof.text:
*$\ker\pi_i\subseteq(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$.* Let $F=(a_E)$ with $\pi_i(F)=0$, i.e. $a_E=0$ for all $E\in S$. For $1\le j\le i$ let $T_j=\{E\in\mathbf N^d:e_1=\cdots=e_{j-1}=0,\ e_j\ge1\}$; every $E
otin S$ lies in exactly one $T_j$ ($j$ the least index $\le i$ with $e_j\ge1$), so $\mathbf N^d$ is the disjoint union of $S,T_1,\ldots,T_i$. Define $G_j=(g^{(j)}_E)\in R$ by $g^{(j)}_E=a_{E+\varepsilon_j}$ if $e_1=\cdots=e_{j-1}=0$ and $g^{(j)}_E=0$ otherwise. By the product formula, for $H\in\mathbf N^d$, $(X_jG_j)_H=\sum_{E'+E=H}(X_j)_{E'}g^{(j)}_E$, and the only nonzero coefficient of $X_j$ is at $E'=\varepsilon_j$; so $(X_jG_j)_H=g^{(j)}_{H-\varepsilon_j}$ if $h_j\ge1$ and $(X_jG_j)_H=0$ if $h_j=0$. Since $H-\varepsilon_j$ and $H$ agree in the entries $1,\ldots,j-1$, this gives $(X_jG_j)_H=a_H$ for $H\in T_j$ and $(X_jG_j)_H=0$ for $H
otin T_j$. Summing coefficientwise over $j=1,\ldots,i$ and using the disjoint decomposition, $(\sum_{j=1}^iX_jG_j)_H=a_H$ for $H
otin S$ and $=0=a_H$ for $H\in S$. Hence $F=\sum_{j=1}^iX_jG_j\in(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$ (for $i=0$: $S=\mathbf N^d$, $F=0$, and the ideal is $0$). With step 4, $\ker\pi_i=(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$.

proof.text: *The quotient and the case $i=d$.* By steps 2, 3 and 5, $\pi_i$ is a surjective $A$-algebra homomorphism $R\to R_i$ with kernel $(X_1,\ldots,X_i)$, so by the first isomorphism theorem for rings it induces an isomorphism of $A$-algebras $R/(X_1,\ldots,X_i)\xrightarrow{\sim}R_i=A[[X_{i+1},\ldots,X_d]]$, $F\bmod(X_1,\ldots,X_i)\mapsto\pi_i(F)$. For $i=d$, $S=\{0\}$ and $R_d=A$ (identified with the series $rX^0$, step 1), and $\pi_d(F)=a_0X^0$ is the constant coefficient $F(0)=a_0$; so $F\mapsto F(0)$, $R\to A$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $(X_1,\ldots,X_d)$.
